indicators.note: The top of a word is the letter it begins with, so only that single letter is taken and the rest is left alone.

parts.note: the letter standing at the top of ENTERTAINER
quips are short jokes

explanation.surface: A leading comedian being handed material to work with.
explanation.walkthrough: Supplies reads as the noun, the boxes of stock a theatre keeps, and it is wanted as the verb. Top marks a first letter just as readily in an across clue as in a down one.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip someone is to supply them with what they need, the two verbs swapping into the same sentence unchanged.

indicators.note: To distribute things is to spread them about among different places, so the letters handed over do not stay where they were.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: Handing round the paperwork for an alliance's round of enquiries.
explanation.walkthrough: NATO in capitals looks like the body doing the asking and is really thirteen letters of raw material with enquiries. The definition is the one short word at the end, easy to read past as part of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A questionnaire is a printed sheet of questions to be filled in and handed back, which is a form.

indicators.note: To capture something is to take it in and hold it, so the word in front closes around the one behind.

parts.note: a figure in a painting or a photograph is an image
what is popular is in, as clothes are in this season

explanation.surface: A public figure catching the mood of the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular fancy' is a real phrase and the clue trades on your reading it as one; fancy is the definition and popular belongs to the wordplay. IN for popular is one of the grid's hardest-working two-letter pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to picture it in the mind — 'fancy that' and 'imagine that' are the same invitation.

indicators.note: In a down clue a thing that rises is read upwards from the bottom, so the letters named come out back to front.

parts.note: the clue's own word, taken as it stands
SATAN climbing a down clue is read from his last letter up

explanation.surface: The devil getting up in the moonlight.
explanation.walkthrough: Moonlight is Beethoven's, and etc quietly widens one famous piece into the whole class it belongs to. A devil climbing a down clue is the setter's excuse for turning his name round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moonlight is Beethoven's best-known sonata, so naming it and adding etc points at the class of pieces rather than at the one.

clue.text: Look now and then to find children's apparatus

parts.note: to look in the present tense is to see
the same verb shifted into the past tense

explanation.surface: An occasional glance round the playground for the children's equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now and then' is a set phrase meaning occasionally, and taking it as two separate times instead is the whole trick. The (3-3) in the count is the warning that two short pieces are coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A see-saw is the pivoted plank children ride at either end, so it is apparatus put there for them.

clue.text: Dance with a doctor in Salvation Army

indicators.note: In sets what comes before it inside what comes after, the outer word splitting open to make room.

parts.note: SA is how the Salvation Army, the uniformed Christian charity, signs itself
the clue's own a, taken as it stands
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is the degree a British doctor qualifies with

explanation.surface: Taking a turn on the dancefloor with a medic from the Salvation Army.
explanation.walkthrough: The Salvation Army is known for brass bands and soup kitchens rather than Latin American dancing, which is what stops the surface giving anything away. Doctor is one of the grid's standard sources of letters, MB or DR or MO depending on the count.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is the Brazilian ballroom dance of the Rio carnival, so Dance names it by the category it belongs to.

clue.text: Woman's going round a part of the roof

indicators.note: Going round a thing means passing on all sides of it, so the letters named close about what follows.

parts.note: Eve, the first woman, with the clue's own S on the end
the clue's own a, taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A woman on her rounds inspecting a stretch of roofing.
explanation.walkthrough: Woman's is a possessive on the surface and is a name plus an S in the wordplay, the apostrophe doing no work at all. Eve is the woman a grid reaches for first, three of her four letters usable.
explanation.definitionFit: The eaves are the overhanging lower edge of a roof, the part the gutter is fixed to.

clue.text: Put out red alert, click for solicitor-to-be

indicators.note: To put something out is to push it out of its proper place, so the letters are set down in an order that is not theirs.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters; the comma is punctuation, not a letter

explanation.surface: Raising the alarm with a single click on a trainee lawyer's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: Put out means upset on the surface and disarranged in the wordplay, the two senses doing quite different jobs in the one sentence. Articles are the training contract a would-be solicitor signs with a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: An articled clerk serves under articles at a law firm, working the training years out before qualifying, so the hyphenated definition names exactly that stage.

clue.text: Yearly hairdo interrupted by a mad nun

indicators.note: Mad means out of its right mind, and letters in that state will not stay in the right order either.
A thing interrupted by another has that other cut into the middle of it and has to carry on afterwards.

parts.note: a perm is a hairdo, the curls set by a permanent wave
the four letters of A NUN rearranged

explanation.surface: A nun losing her mind in the middle of somebody's yearly trip to the salon.
explanation.walkthrough: Yearly is an adverb and so is the Latin phrase wanted, which is why the definition can sit flush against the wordplay without a joining word. Mad is there twice over: as the word that muddles the letters and as the reason the nun is interrupting anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Per annum is the Latin the bank and the payslip use for by the year, so yearly says it in English.

indicators.note: Upsetting something tips it over and spills what was inside, so the letters do not come out as they went in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A ballot overturning somebody's block on a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder and the answer are near-opposites, one killing a decision and the other making it, which is the quiet joke here. Four-letter anagrams are the hardest to see precisely because there is so little to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A vote is the choice cast in an election, and ballot carries the same sense of the count itself — a firm puts a strike to a ballot.

indicators.note: Kept in says the letters wanted are being held inside the word that follows, in the order they already stand there.

parts.note: perpETUIty, four letters running on across the middle of one long word

explanation.surface: A little box that nobody is ever going to part with.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a Victorian lady's needle-case, kept alive almost entirely by crosswords, so learning it once pays out for years. Perpetuity is chosen because nothing about for ever suggests a container.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is the small ornamental case a Victorian woman carried needles, scissors and bodkins in.

indicators.note: Someone indisposed is out of sorts, and letters out of sorts are letters no longer in their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; the apostrophe counts for nothing

explanation.surface: A leading actor too unwell to go on tonight.
explanation.walkthrough: An apostrophe is thrown away freely in anagram fodder, which is worth knowing before you count letters twice. The definition sits right against can't, exactly where the eye refuses to make a break.
explanation.definitionFit: To transact business is to carry it through, and perform covers that same sense of getting a piece of business done.

clue.text: Knight loves unusual works of fiction

indicators.note: Unusual means not as it usually is, so the letters in front of it are taken out of their usual order.

parts.note: N is the knight in chess notation
the five letters of LOVES rearranged

explanation.surface: A knight with a taste for odd stories.
explanation.walkthrough: N for knight comes from chess, where K is already spoken for by the king. The surface runs as one unbroken sentence about somebody's reading, which is what hides the break after loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Novels are book-length invented stories, the plain name for works of fiction.

clue.text: Soundly spoke and rang a bell

indicators.note: Soundly points at the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so what is wanted is something said the same way.

parts.note: spoke is TOLD, and the answer is said exactly that way while being spelt nothing like it

explanation.surface: Somebody spoke firmly and set a bell ringing.
explanation.walkthrough: Identical in the mouth, unrelated on the page — that gap is all a homophone needs. The definition wants the slow single strokes rung for a death rather than any old ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: To toll a bell is to ring it in slow measured strokes, as at a funeral, so rang a bell matches it in tense and sense.

indicators.note: To broadcast is to scatter seed by hand across a field, and letters scattered that way land in no set order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A dreary bit of television filmed away from the studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside broadcast' is the British television term for filming on location, and the clue is built so the two words read as that one thing. Broadcast in its farming sense is why it works as an instruction to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious drags on without variation, which is what monotonous describes.

clue.text: Tell fibs about drink being cordial

indicators.note: About means round the outside of a thing, so the word before it wraps itself around what comes next.

parts.note: to tell fibs is to lie
mead is the honey wine of Anglo-Saxon feasting halls

explanation.surface: Someone lying about how much they have had, and pleasant enough with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Cordial is the trap: it reads as the adjective for friendly and is wanted as a noun. In Britain a cordial is the concentrated fruit syrup you dilute from the bottle, not an American after-dinner liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Limeade is lime sweetened and watered down, exactly the sort of fruit drink a British kitchen calls a cordial.

clue.text: International with foolish pride, but valiant

indicators.note: Something foolish is not sensibly arranged, so the letters it points at are not left in a sensible order.

parts.note: int is the standard short form of international, as on a fixture list
the five letters of PRIDE rearranged

explanation.surface: A player capped for his country, vain to the point of silliness and brave all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: But is the hinge the clue depends on: it makes foolish pride and bravery sound like a contrast being drawn about one man, when foolish is only an instruction. Pride and the answer do keep company in life, which helps the sentence hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone intrepid presses on where others would turn back, which is what valiant says of a person.

clue.text: One who gets up part of the stairs?

definitions.meaning: somebody out of bed before the rest of the house, an early one of these
the upright board closing the gap between one tread and the next

explanation.surface: Somebody who has climbed only part of the staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing the work: read straight through, the clue paints one person part-way up a flight, and the two halves have to be cut apart between up and part. A staircase is treads to stand on with uprights between them.
explanation.definitionFit: An early riser is one who gets out of bed, and a stair's riser is the upright board between two treads.

definitions.meaning: first in rank, as the minister is
getting a wall or a pump ready before it can do its job

explanation.surface: Getting ready is the thing that matters most of all.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one piece of advice and has to be broken after important, the halves turning out to be an adjective and a verb. Priming a wall is the undercoat that goes on before the paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Prime means first in rank or quality, which is most important; to prime a surface, a pump or a bomb is to prepare it.

definitions.meaning: to jeer at somebody, laughing in order to wound
sham, counterfeit, standing in for the real thing

explanation.surface: Making fun of something fake.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses laid end to end with nothing between them, which is why the clue is only three words long. The imitation sense is the one in a school's practice exam and in the old soup that never saw a turtle.
explanation.definitionFit: To mock is to jeer at someone, and a mock diamond or a mock exam is an imitation of the real thing.

indicators.note: Almost all of a word is all of it bar the end, so the last letter is left off.

parts.note: FIRST means original and gives up its last letter

explanation.surface: A stand of trees that are not quite the original planting.
explanation.walkthrough: Original and first are synonyms in the sense of earliest, and that pairing is worth carrying about. Almost is the plain instruction to stop one letter short.
explanation.definitionFit: Firs are the tall evergreen conifers of northern forests and Christmas, so trees names them by their class.

parts.note: the clue's own pronoun, taken as it stands
to do somebody is British slang for cheating them — 'I've been done'
later means afterwards

explanation.surface: A fan the speaker fully intends to con in due course.
explanation.walkthrough: Done meaning cheated rather than finished is the slang the middle of this turns on. The definition is a single hyphenated word at the front, which is the place the eye is least willing to cut.
explanation.definitionFit: An idolater worships an idol, and the word is used of anyone who adores a person past all reason — a hero-worshipper.

definitions.meaning: the qualification a university confers at the end of a course
extent or magnitude, the sense in which a thing happens on a large one

explanation.surface: A university qualification pitched somewhere on a sliding scale.
explanation.walkthrough: On looks like it is placing one thing upon another and is only joining two definitions. The second sense wanted is extent or magnitude, not the ruler's markings and not the fish's.
explanation.definitionFit: A degree is the qualification a university awards, and it also means extent — to a large degree and on a large scale say the same thing.

indicators.note: Anything on board a vessel is within it, so the word before goes inside the ship that follows.

parts.note: SS is the prefix on a steamship's name, as in SS Great Britain
teak is the hardwood timber traditionally laid as ships' decking

explanation.surface: Sawing lengths of wood up on the deck of a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Cuts is the trap: the sawing that timber invites is the wrong sense, and the butcher's is the right one. Teak was the decking wood of choice at sea, which is what lets the surface hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak is a thick slice carved off a carcass, so Cuts names them the way a butcher's counter does.
